frameworks.name: Daily Sales Training Cadence
frameworks.definition: A 30-minute daily training block scheduled at the lowest-probability sales hour, covering a rotating weekly script section (intro/discovery/pitch/close Mon-Thu, hot topic Fri), with manager modeling followed by paired role-play.

frameworks.name: Three-Part One-on-One Structure
frameworks.definition: Weekly manager-rep one-on-one split into personal check-in, short-term quota and call review, and long-term career development — in that sequence and skipping later sections only when earlier ones reveal critical issues.

frameworks.name: Bimodal Sales Career Ladder
frameworks.definition: A six-level career progression (junior setter -> setter -> senior setter -> junior closer -> closer -> senior closer) that gives reps incremental title, pay, and perk milestones tied to gross output rather than tenure.

frameworks.name: Three-Milestone Sales On-Ramp
frameworks.definition: New talking-role hires must sequentially pass: (1) full script memorization, (2) recap/labeling skill, and (3) close and objection handling — each gated by a manager test before the next phase unlocks.

frameworks.name: Blackout Script Memorization Method
frameworks.definition: Print two copies of the script; say it aloud, black out one word, say it again — repeat until the entire script is blacked out. The number of words equals the number of repetitions.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in a sales team, the sales manager is always ultimately responsible for the team's behavior: if the sales team is not doing what is required, it is because the sales manager is not doing what they need to be doing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any sales team with a dedicated manager
claims.mechanism: Culture and standards in a department are set top-down by the leader; without manager modeling the desired behavior, reps have no authoritative reference to emulate.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi structures daily sales training as a mandatory 30-minute block scheduled at the team's lowest-probability sales hour (10:00-10:30 AM PST for his teams), with the only permitted absence being an actively open closing call that bleeds into the window.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: inside sales teams with predictable low-volume hours
claims.mechanism: Scheduling training at the lowest-demand sales window minimizes revenue opportunity cost while keeping the daily habit inviolable.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a weekly sales script curriculum must cycle through all four script sections — intro, discovery, pitch, and close — rather than drilling a single section, because drilling only one section causes the other sections to degrade and produce the problem the drill was meant to fix.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: scripted sales roles with a multi-part call structure
claims.mechanism: Each section of a sales call sets up the next; reps who struggle with objections (close) often do so because they mishandled the intro, so drilling only the close does not remove the root cause — it requires sharpening the whole sword weekly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the most expensive mistake in running a sales team is allowing untrained reps to work live leads: the short-term cost of 30 minutes of daily training is far lower than the revenue destroyed by leads burned by untrained reps.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: inbound or paid-lead environments where lead cost is material
claims.mechanism: Untrained reps convert at structurally lower rates and may permanently damage prospects who would have closed under a trained rep, destroying both the immediate deal and future referral value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses a Blackout Script Memorization method in which reps say a script aloud, black out one word, say it again, and repeat until every word is blacked out; this means a 400-word script requires approximately 400 repetitions before a rep speaks to any live prospect.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: talking-based sales roles with a fixed script
claims.mechanism: Incremental word-by-word deletion forces active recall at each step rather than passive reading, and the number of repetitions equals the script length — ensuring words become automatic before live-call pressure is introduced.

numbers.axis: script repetitions required before live calls

bounded_by: reps do this self-directed, not with manager time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi gates new sales reps from live leads entirely until they pass all three on-ramp milestones sequentially; upon passing, they receive a half-calendar of leads and must hit KPI for five consecutive days before receiving a full calendar.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: inbound lead environments with measurable cost-per-lead
claims.mechanism: Leads are the most expensive resource in the sales funnel; allowing an unproven rep to burn leads before demonstrating readiness destroys more value than the delay costs.
bounded_by: reps who fail KPI in second half-ramp are exited

claims.text: Alex Hormozi structures the first 30-day promotion for a new sales rep as a guaranteed raise (not title change) requiring only that the rep completes the first month and meets the basics — the primary purpose is to give them a win to report to family, not to reward exceptional performance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: new hire in a sales role, within first 30 days
claims.mechanism: Early positive reinforcement anchors the rep's identity with the role and the company before the harder work begins; a small concrete win sustains motivation through the steep part of the learning curve.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi ties career advancement in the six-stage sales ladder to cumulative gross output (number of deals closed or sets made), not tenure, so that high-performers can compress a 4.5-year path to 18 months by working nights and weekends.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales roles with measurable per-deal output
claims.mechanism: Output-based promotion creates a direct incentive to work higher volume: pulling the future forward by closing 100 deals in two months instead of six months accelerates advancement and total compensation.

numbers.axis: time to complete six-stage career ladder

bounded_by: KPI must be paired — volume alone without quality threshold does not qualify for advancement

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that any output-based KPI used for sales promotion must be paired with an antagonist quality metric (e.g., close rate paired with volume, or session count paired with five-star reviews), because a single metric creates an incentive to hit volume at the expense of quality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any role with a repeatable measurable output: sales, clinical, editorial
claims.mechanism: Unpaired metrics create perverse incentives; a rep who knows advancement requires only deal count will burn leads to maximize attempts, destroying LTV. Pairing volume with a quality floor neutralizes this at the system level.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in the weekly team meeting (distinct from the one-on-one), the primary exercise is reviewing recorded call footage in front of the full team — not lecture — so that correction is applied to real game footage and becomes a shared team learning event.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Observing a peer's real call, rather than a hypothetical script, surfaces live objection patterns and removes the rep's defensive rationalization that training scenarios are unrealistic.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi structures the one-on-one review around three calls that the rep pre-selects as their hardest or most instructive cases from that week, so that the manager's coaching is targeted to the specific failure pattern of that individual rather than generic team issues.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: one-on-one between sales manager and individual rep
claims.mechanism: Rep-selected calls surface the rep's own blind spots and motivate them to engage because they chose the material; manager-selected calls often feel arbitrary and generate defensiveness.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that at very high repetition counts (citing his own practice of complex presentations), learning has distinct phases: around repetition 10 initial comprehension begins, by repetition 40 the overall structure is internalized, and from 40 to 80 micro-transitions and timing refinements emerge — implying that most practitioners stop before the high-value phase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: complex scripted performance: sales pitch, keynote presentation, or multi-step demonstration
claims.mechanism: Early repetitions build word-level fluency; mid repetitions reveal structural logic; late repetitions expose micro-optimizations invisible at lower rep counts. Each phase unlocks the next, making stopping early structurally invisible — the learner does not know what they are missing.
bounded_by: speaker cites personal experience with a 1,700-slide, 2-hour scripted presentation; may not generalize to all skill types

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a senior setter role should carry non-monetary perks — such as no weekend requirement or no late-shift requirement — that are valued by the rep and unavailable at lower levels, because these perks make the title change self-evidently worth achieving without requiring large salary jumps.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales or service roles with predictable schedule grievances (weekends, late shifts, undesirable locations)
claims.mechanism: Converting the things reps chronically complain about (bad shifts, commute, no choice of scheduling) into achievement-unlockable perks turns shared frustrations into motivation; the perk is worth more in perceived value than its equivalent monetary cost because it addresses a daily pain point.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a bimodal career ladder applied to non-sales roles (e.g., nail technicians, clinicians, editors) with skill-gated progression — where each level requires learning a new skill rather than just accruing time — enables paying practitioners twice the industry-average wage while maintaining retention rates far above industry norms.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: labor-intensive service roles with teachable skill hierarchies
claims.mechanism: Skill-gated advancement aligns wage growth with billable value growth; as the practitioner's skill increases their revenue per hour for the business, higher wages are self-funded. Retention is anchored by the career horizon rather than immediate compensation alone.
bounded_by: requires that skills are genuinely teachable in sequence and that higher-skill work commands higher prices

examples.text: Alex Hormozi described his preparation for a 1,700-slide, two-hour scripted presentation at a Money Models launch event. Every word spoken was on screen — nothing was improvised. Beyond memorizing the verbal script, Hormozi had to practice the physical choreography simultaneously: clicking slides with one hand while unboxing a complex product display, setting up trays, and positioning books so their pages would not fall — a coordination failure he experienced multiple times in rehearsal. He then had to duct-tape items to weight them correctly. He described that had he only practiced the verbal content without also rehearsing the physical execution, he would have discovered critical coordination failures on stage in front of the audience for the first time. He used this as evidence that practitioners wildly underestimate the volume of work required for high-quality performance.

Alex Hormozi recounted a nail salon chain he and a business partner (JJ) made an offer on. The owner had developed a tiered skill progression for nail technicians: each level required mastering a new decorative technique (e.g., stars, then small illustrations), which also increased each tech's billable rate per service. The progression meant the salon owner only had to train the most basic skill at onboarding, and deeper training was unlocked only after the tech demonstrated they would stay past a certain tenure threshold. By the time techs reached the higher tiers, they were earning approximately $75,000 per year — roughly twice the industry average for nail technicians. The owner retained her staff for years, and her techs were substantially more skilled than competitors' staff. Hormozi cited this as the exemplary application of output-gated, skill-linked career progression to a non-sales service role.

practices.text: Open every daily sales team meeting with manager-delivered kudos (specific call-outs of individual rep behavior to reinforce) followed by peer-to-peer shout-outs before moving to role-play.
On Friday training sessions, replace the rotating script-section drill with a hot-topic session focused on whatever objection or failure pattern the team encountered most that week.
In the role-play portion of daily training, have the manager model the section first, then do it with one rep to lock in the standard, then break the full team into pairs to practice with each other.

For any repeated headcount role (sales, customer success, editors), design a junior/senior split at each existing level to create six promotion milestones rather than two, giving reps visible advancement at frequent intervals.

New talking-role hires should spend the first week alternating between ride-alongs (observing live sales calls) and solo script memorization using the Blackout method, then complete two days of direct manager coaching before any live lead exposure.
If a new rep cannot pass the script-memorization milestone within two to three days of attempts, do not advance them further — exit them rather than spending lead budget on an under-prepared rep.
Require reps to submit three calls they found difficult before each one-on-one so the manager can diagnose the specific failure pattern in advance rather than diagnosing cold during the meeting.

Only move to the long-term career discussion portion of a one-on-one if the rep is hitting quota and their personal life is stable; if either is compromised, focus the entire session on the lower-level need.
